first_impression.reaction: The opening line is nice and calm: 'It starts weeks or months earlier, in a living room, when one family visits another to ask a question.' No 'fairytale', no 'dream day'. Then it tells us straight away it's for Lebanese-Australian and mixed-heritage couples taking this abroad, which is us. The headline is a bit clickbaity ('You Did Not Know?') but the page underneath isn't, so we kept going.

journey.quote: Lebanese families are Christian, Muslim and Druze, so ask each side which customs they actually keep before you plan the programme.
journey.reaction: First sensible thing anyone has said to us. James's side and my side will want different bits, and this doesn't pretend there's one checklist.

journey.quote: For a wedding abroad, a smaller engagement dinner can work well as an early welcome for guests who arrive a few days before, so the families meet before the big night.
journey.reaction: Practical. That's a real planning idea, not just a definition.

journey.quote: In Arab weddings generally, the families reading the Fatiha after the father agrees is described as typically accompanied by Arabic coffee in the Levant, though that account is framed around Muslim families in Egypt, Palestine and Jordan rather than Lebanon.
journey.reaction: We get that they're being careful, but 'in Arab weddings generally... is described as... though that account is framed around...' is a mouthful. It happens a few times in the early sections and it reads like a footnote, not a guide. We'd rather one clear sentence and a line saying families differ.

journey.section: The church ceremony and the crowning
journey.quote: The Melkite Greek Catholic Eparchy of Newton calls the Eastern Churches' marriage service the Mystery of Crowning.
journey.reaction: This section is thorough but heavy. Two church sources, Ephesians, Cana, St John Chrysostom. Our parents might read it; we skimmed to the next heading. Honestly the useful bit is 'Your priest is the person to ask.'

journey.section: The church ceremony and the crowning
journey.quote: One line stands out for Lebanese couples: a crowning prayer in the Orthodox text asks God to "exalt them like the cedars of Lebanon, like a luxuriant vine".
journey.reaction: Lovely. That's going in the order of service, and it's the bit I'd send to Mum.

journey.quote: For a picture of how it feels, see [a glamorous traditional Lebanese wedding in Sydney](/real-wedding-a-glamorous-and-traditional-wedding).
journey.reaction: Real weddings linked from inside the article, not just a hero shot. That's what we look for.

journey.section: Bringing Lebanese customs to a wedding abroad
journey.quote: For two real examples, see [a traditional Lebanese wedding on Lake Como](/a-traditional-lebanese-destination-wedding-in-lake-como-italy) and [a Lebanese couple's medieval-style wedding in Italy](/a-lebanese-medieval-destination-wedding-in-italy).
journey.reaction: Two destination real weddings with Lebanese couples. This is the thing that moves us from reading to clicking around the site. We'll open both.

journey.section: Space for the zaffeh and the dabke line
journey.quote: Ask the venue for the floor's real dimensions once tables are set, and whether a terrace can take the overflow.
journey.reaction: Insider detail. Nobody else has told us the floor shrinks once tables go in. Same with the drum and music finish time point.

journey.section: Timing a henna night around travel
journey.quote: For a destination wedding, that usually means two nights before the wedding, leaving the night before free for rest and a rehearsal.
journey.reaction: Exactly the kind of sequencing we'd otherwise be working out on a spreadsheet. Useful.

journey.section: Blades, venue rules and the cake
journey.quote: If a family heirloom is travelling with you, check your airline's rules and the destination's rules on carrying a blade well ahead of the flight.
journey.reaction: Ha, we wouldn't have thought of that until check-in. Good catch.

journey.section: Blades, venue rules and the cake
journey.quote: Your Advisor is a single point of contact who plans the venue, travel and vendors, agrees the fee in writing before any work begins, and confirms what is included in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: Better than the usual 'end-to-end'. Single point of contact and fee in writing up front speaks to our hidden-cost worry. Still doesn't say whether 'travel' means our 45 international guests and grandparents getting from the airport, or just us.

journey.section: A note on travel and marriage law
journey.quote: You can't register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is recognised if it was valid where it happened and would have been valid under Australian law.
journey.reaction: Clear, sourced and honest that it's not legal advice. The Lebanon travel warning and dual-national point are things James's parents need to hear from someone other than us.

unanswered_questions: When the Advisor 'plans travel', does that cover guest travel and airport transfers for 60 to 90 people, or only the couple?
Can Wedded Wonderland source drummers for a zaffeh, a dabke troupe, a henna artist or a Lebanese sweets caterer in Italy, or do we fly people in?
If we want a crowning in Italy, does the Advisor help find an Eastern-rite priest or parish near the venue, and how does that sit with the legal marriage there?
Across a multi-evening week (engagement dinner, henna night, wedding), who is on the ground and accountable on each night?
would_share_with: Parents (the cedars of Lebanon prayer, the Smartraveller and dual-nationality section)
Grandparents via parents (the tulbeh and henna sections)

cta_reaction.quote: If you would like one person to hold all of this together, you can [speak with a Wedded Advisor](/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=lebanese-wedding-traditions&utm_content=secondary).
cta_reaction.why: 'One person to hold all of this together' is exactly what we want and it's not pushy. We'd read the Lake Como real wedding first, share this with the parents, then probably enquire after another post or two.

top_3_changes: Add one concrete line on what the Advisor does for guests across a multi-day celebration (airport transfers, transport between evenings, someone accountable on each night), since 'travel' is ambiguous.

Trim the stacked hedging in the tulbeh, engagement and katb al-kitab sections ('In Arab weddings generally... is described as... though that account is framed around...') to one clear sentence plus 'families differ'.
Tighten the crowning section so the planning point (clear aisle, ask your priest, the cedars line) comes before the liturgical detail; most of us will skim the source list.
